For Heidegger, technology is not fundamentally a collection of tools but a *way of revealing*—a mode through which beings become intelligible and present to human beings. His account draws on the Greek term *alētheia*, commonly translated as “truth” but more literally suggestive of unconcealment: something comes out of concealment and appears. Truth in this sense is not merely the correctness of a statement about an already fixed object. It is the prior opening in which something can show itself as something at all. Human beings participate in this revealing, but they do not simply invent or control it. A historical mode of revealing “sends” or directs how the real can appear. Heidegger calls this sending *destining* (*Geschick*). Thus technology is a human way of revealing reality not because people freely impose any meaning they choose, but because a historically specific understanding guides what they notice, value, and make accessible.

Heidegger distinguishes the revealing characteristic of modern technology from the “bringing-forth” (*poiēsis*) associated with ancient craft and nature. Bringing-forth allows something to emerge into presence—for example, a craftsperson helps a work take shape, while a plant grows according to its own powers. Modern technological revealing, by contrast, is “challenging-forth”: it demands that nature yield energy, materials, and information in calculable, continuously available forms. A river appears as a source of hydroelectric power, a forest as timber inventory, and even human capacities as measurable resources. Heidegger names the resulting mode of appearance *standing-reserve* (*Bestand*). This does not mean that the river or forest ceases to exist physically; rather, the technological framework makes its resource-character especially salient and tends to obscure other ways it might matter. Modern technology therefore discloses real features of beings, but it also narrows the field of disclosure by privileging availability, efficiency, and control.

The connection to *veritas* clarifies what Heidegger sees as historically distinctive in familiar ideas of truth. In ordinary usage, truth is often treated as the correctness of a representation: a proposition is true when it accurately corresponds to an object. Heidegger does not simply reject this sense; he argues that it depends on a more basic disclosure of beings as objects that can be represented and measured. The modern technological destining helps make that objectifying stance seem self-evident, and it enables the historical world to appear as a record of observable events available to historiography. Yet *alētheia* reminds us that every regime of correctness rests on a prior way in which things are allowed to show up—and that every revealing also conceals. Heidegger’s point, then, is not that technology is unreal or merely harmful, but that its mode of truth is neither neutral nor exhaustive. Recognizing its destining can make room for other forms of revealing, including attentive, artistic, and contemplative relations in which beings are not encountered only as resources.

Sexual differentiation of the brain is not a single event synchronized with genital development. In typical mammalian development, chromosomal sex influences gonadal differentiation, and the fetal testes may then produce testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone. Androgens act through the androgen receptor, while testosterone can be converted by aromatase to estradiol; in several animal models, this locally produced estrogen is a major organizer of sex-typical neural development. The timing, concentration, metabolism, and cellular sensitivity to these signals vary among tissues. Genital structures respond during an earlier, relatively defined prenatal window, whereas some neural circuits develop or remain plastic later. Brain regions also differ in receptor expression, local enzyme activity, gene regulation, and developmental origin. Thus, a neural region need not follow the same trajectory as external anatomy, and “brain sex” is not a single, uniform trait. Genetic variation in hormone synthesis or receptor function, epigenetic regulation, and prenatal conditions that affect hormone availability or action are plausible contributors to variation. These mechanisms are well supported in broad terms, particularly by animal research, but their specific roles in human variation in structures such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and INAH3 remain incompletely established.

Postmortem studies have reported group-average differences in features such as BSTc volume or cell number and INAH3 size, with some findings suggesting that these measures in transgender people are closer to averages reported for their experienced gender than for their sex assigned at birth. Such results are relevant but must be interpreted cautiously. Sample sizes have often been small, the regions are difficult to measure, and results may be affected by age, hormone treatment, illness, or other factors; findings across studies are not wholly consistent. Further, group differences do not reliably classify individuals, and a region’s size or cell count cannot be assumed to cause a particular identity. Human studies generally cannot establish whether a measured brain feature preceded identity, resulted partly from later experience or treatment, or reflects a third developmental influence. Prenatal hormone exposure is therefore a plausible part of a multifactorial account, not a demonstrated single explanation. Genetic, hormonal, epigenetic, and experiential influences may interact, and evidence from animal models cannot be transferred directly to complex human identity.

The evidence does not demonstrate that gender identity is “hardwired” before birth if that term means fixed, fully specified, or biologically inevitable. It does support the more limited possibility that prenatal development contributes to enduring predispositions in neural systems relevant to sex-typed behavior, body perception, or identity. “Hardwired” is especially misleading because brains continue to develop after birth, neural traits are distributed across networks rather than located in one nucleus, and biological influence is compatible with variation and developmental plasticity. Identity is a complex human phenomenon, not a direct readout of BSTc or INAH3 anatomy. The most defensible conclusion is that prenatal biology may contribute to gender identity for some people, alongside later developmental and social influences, but the mechanisms and their relative importance remain unsettled. Current neuroanatomical findings are suggestive evidence for developmental diversity, not proof of a prenatal neural blueprint or a definitive biological test of anyone’s identity.

A key step in Wiles’s strategy is to connect the hypothetical Fermat counterexample to the modularity of elliptic curves. If a nontrivial solution to \(a^n+b^n=c^n\) existed for a prime exponent \(n>2\), the Frey construction would associate to it a particular semistable elliptic curve. Ribet’s theorem implies that this curve cannot be modular. Consequently, it is enough to establish that every semistable elliptic curve over the rationals is modular: the Frey curve would then have to be both modular and non-modular, a contradiction. This argument does not prove Fermat’s Last Theorem by directly ruling out each possible set of integers; instead, it translates the existence of any counterexample into a statement about elliptic curves and modular forms, where powerful structural theorems can be applied.

Wiles’s modularity argument is organized around Galois representations attached to elliptic curves. For a prime \(p\), an elliptic curve \(E\) gives a representation \(\rho_{E,p}\), describing how the absolute Galois group of the rationals acts on the curve’s points of order \(p\). Roughly, modularity of this representation means that it arises from a modular form. Wiles sought to prove a modularity-lifting theorem: under suitable hypotheses, if the representation modulo \(p\) is modular, then the compatible representations describing the \(p\)-power torsion—often considered as a \(p\)-adic representation—are modular as well. Since modularity of the elliptic curve is encoded by this \(p\)-adic representation, such a result allows modularity to be established by studying a comparatively accessible representation modulo \(p\), rather than proving it directly at every higher power of \(p\). The prime is chosen to make the necessary hypotheses and arguments work; it is not simply arbitrary, because the lifting theorem has specific conditions.

The technical heart of this approach is the deformation method. One fixes a residual representation, such as \(\bar\rho_{E,p}\), and studies its possible lifts to representations over progressively richer coefficient rings, subject to conditions reflecting the arithmetic of the elliptic curve. These allowed lifts are organized by a deformation ring. In parallel, modular forms give rise to a Hecke algebra that records the relevant modular lifts. Wiles’s central comparison identifies these two structures—schematically, by showing that the deformation ring and Hecke algebra match—so that the permitted Galois representations can be shown to come from modular forms. Reducibility matters because the residual representation can split into simpler pieces or remain irreducible, and the available lifting arguments differ in these cases. Wiles’s work, together with the subsequent repair by Taylor and Wiles, established the needed results for semistable elliptic curves and thereby supplied the modularity contradiction that proves Fermat’s Last Theorem.

La diferenciación sexual del cerebro prenatal no es una copia tardía de la diferenciación genital: ambos procesos pueden responder a señales hormonales y genéticas parcialmente distintas, en momentos sensibles diferentes y con grados variables de sensibilidad tisular. En el desarrollo típico masculino, la expresión de **SRY** en la gónada embrionaria activa una cascada genética —entre otros factores, **SOX9**— que favorece la formación de testículos. Estos producen testosterona y hormona antimülleriana; en algunos tejidos, la enzima aromatasa convierte testosterona en estradiol. En numerosos mamíferos, el estradiol derivado de testosterona es una señal importante para masculinizar ciertos circuitos cerebrales, mientras que en humanos la contribución relativa de andrógenos, estrógenos y mecanismos independientes de hormonas sigue siendo objeto de investigación. Las hormonas actúan mediante receptores cuya distribución varía entre regiones y células; además, diferencias en genes reguladores, metabolismo hormonal, epigenética y momento de exposición pueden modificar la respuesta local. Por ello, una estructura cerebral puede seguir una trayectoria que no coincida exactamente con la de los genitales externos o con otras características corporales. No se trata, sin embargo, de un mecanismo único ni de una simple “dosis” hormonal: importan la temporalidad, la sensibilidad del tejido y la interacción entre genes, hormonas y ambiente intrauterino.

El **BSTc** (subdivisión central del núcleo de la estría terminal) y el **INAH3** (tercer núcleo intersticial del hipotálamo anterior) se han estudiado por diferencias promedio asociadas al sexo en tamaño, número celular u otros rasgos, así como por posibles variaciones relacionadas con la identidad de género. Algunos estudios post mortem comunicaron que ciertas medidas del BSTc en mujeres trans se aproximaban más a los promedios observados en mujeres cis que a los de hombres cis; trabajos sobre INAH3 han descrito patrones parcialmente concordantes, aunque no uniformes. Estos resultados son sugerentes, pero no establecen una causa prenatal ni un “marcador” individual: las muestras han sido pequeñas y seleccionadas, las definiciones y mediciones varían, y tratamientos hormonales, edad, salud y otros factores pueden influir en el tejido. Además, hay solapamiento considerable entre grupos y diferencias medias no permiten inferir la identidad de una persona. Las condiciones intersexuales y los estudios de exposición prenatal a hormonas ofrecen indicios de que la señalización endocrina temprana puede influir en algunos aspectos del desarrollo psicosexual, pero no permiten atribuir la identidad de género a una hormona o estructura aislada. También se investigan efectos de genes expresados directamente en el cerebro, la placenta, el estrés materno y otras condiciones intrauterinas; para muchos de estos factores, la evidencia humana es limitada o correlacional.

Por tanto, la investigación no demuestra que la identidad de género esté “cableada” de manera fija y completa antes del nacimiento. “Cableado” es una metáfora engañosa: el cerebro se desarrolla mediante procesos plásticos, escalonados y sensibles a la experiencia, y la identidad de género es un fenómeno complejo que no se reduce a la anatomía de unas pocas regiones. La interpretación más prudente es que factores biológicos prenatales pueden contribuir a la variación de rasgos cerebrales y, posiblemente, a aspectos de la identidad, junto con procesos del desarrollo posteriores y contextos sociales; su peso relativo y sus mecanismos precisos siguen sin resolverse. Esta postura evita dos conclusiones excesivas: que la identidad sea una decisión voluntaria sin bases biológicas, o que estudios anatómicos limitados prueben un destino prenatal inmutable. La evidencia disponible respalda una etiología multifactorial y probabilística, no una explicación única ni un test biológico capaz de determinar la identidad de género de una persona.

```python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

texts = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,"
]

# Character n-grams capture spelling and subword patterns, which is useful
# for short texts and French inflections. Strip accents and lowercase first.
vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(
    analyzer="char",
    ngram_range=(2, 5),
    lowercase=True,
    strip_accents="unicode",
    norm="l2"
)

vectors = vectorizer.fit_transform(texts)
similarities = cosine_similarity(vectors)

for i, text in enumerate(texts):
    # Exclude the text itself, whose similarity to itself is 1.
    scores = similarities[i].copy()
    scores[i] = -1.0
    neighbor = scores.argmax()

    print(f"Text {i + 1}: {text}")
    print(f"  Nearest neighbor: {texts[neighbor]}")
    print(f"  Cosine similarity: {similarities[i, neighbor]:.4f}\n")
```

The script represents each text as a sparse TF–IDF vector of character n-grams. A character n-gram is a contiguous sequence of *n* characters: for example, the word *amour* contributes fragments such as *am*, *amo*, and *mour* when the selected range is two to five characters. Unlike word-based features, character n-grams do not require tokenization into whole words and can register shared prefixes, suffixes, and internal spellings. This is useful for short literary lines, where a few overlapping words or inflectional endings can be informative, and it is relatively tolerant of spelling variation. Lowercasing avoids treating capitalization as a distinction, while Unicode accent stripping maps accented and unaccented forms to the same normalized character representation. The n-gram range is configurable: shorter fragments capture common local patterns, while longer ones provide more specific evidence of shared sequences.

TF–IDF weights the n-grams before comparison. Term frequency reflects how strongly an n-gram is represented in a particular line; inverse document frequency reduces the influence of n-grams that occur in many lines and therefore distinguish them less well. In scikit-learn, the resulting vectors are L2-normalized by default (also specified explicitly here), so each nonzero vector has unit length. Because most possible character n-grams do not occur in any given line, these representations are sparse: they store only the features that actually appear rather than a dense value for every possible feature. The vectorizer learns its feature vocabulary from the supplied corpus, so the comparisons are relative to these ten texts.

The script calculates pairwise cosine similarity between every pair of vectors. For vectors \(x_i\) and \(x_j\), cosine similarity is \((x_i \cdot x_j) / (\|x_i\|\|x_j\|)\); it is higher when the texts share more heavily weighted n-grams in similar proportions. With L2-normalized vectors, this is their dot product. The resulting matrix contains one score for each pair, and the diagonal consists of self-similarities, normally 1.0. For each line, the script excludes that diagonal entry and selects the remaining line with the highest score. Thus, “nearest” means most similar under this particular TF–IDF character n-gram representation and cosine metric, not necessarily closest in meaning, authorship, or literary theme. The printed score makes the ranking inspectable; ties are resolved by the first maximum returned by NumPy.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# babel.sh
# Usage: ./babel.sh BOOK_INDEX PAGE_INDEX [START_OFFSET [LENGTH]]
#
# Indices and offsets are zero-based. START_OFFSET and LENGTH count characters
# within the page. The full library has 25^(410*80) books, each with 410 pages
# of 80 characters (25^80 possible pages).

set -euo pipefail

if (( $# < 2 || $# > 4 )); then
  echo "Usage: $0 BOOK_INDEX PAGE_INDEX [START_OFFSET [LENGTH]]" >&2
  exit 2
fi

python3 - "$@" <<'PY'
import sys

ALPHABET = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz., "  # 26 letters, period, comma, space
PAGE_CHARS = 80
PAGES_PER_BOOK = 410

def nonnegative_decimal(text, name):
    if not text.isascii() or not text.isdecimal():
        raise SystemExit(f"{name} must be a nonnegative decimal integer")
    return int(text)

book = nonnegative_decimal(sys.argv[1], "BOOK_INDEX")
page = nonnegative_decimal(sys.argv[2], "PAGE_INDEX")
start = nonnegative_decimal(sys.argv[3], "START_OFFSET") if len(sys.argv) >= 4 else 0
length = nonnegative_decimal(sys.argv[4], "LENGTH") if len(sys.argv) >= 5 else PAGE_CHARS

if page >= PAGES_PER_BOOK:
    raise SystemExit(f"PAGE_INDEX must be between 0 and {PAGES_PER_BOOK - 1}")
if start > PAGE_CHARS:
    raise SystemExit(f"START_OFFSET must be between 0 and {PAGE_CHARS}")

# Treat each book as one base-25 number, with its first character most
# significant. The page number selects a fixed-width block of 80 digits.
book_digits = PAGE_CHARS * PAGES_PER_BOOK
if book >= 25 ** book_digits:
    raise SystemExit("BOOK_INDEX is outside the finite library")

page_value = book // (25 ** (PAGE_CHARS * (PAGES_PER_BOOK - 1 - page)))
page_value %= 25 ** PAGE_CHARS

# Decode the page number into exactly 80 base-25 digits, preserving leading
# zeroes; digit 0 maps to 'a', digit 24 to a space.
chars = ["a"] * PAGE_CHARS
for i in range(PAGE_CHARS - 1, -1, -1):
    page_value, digit = divmod(page_value, 25)
    chars[i] = ALPHABET[digit]

sys.stdout.write("".join(chars[start:start + length]) + "\n")
PY
```

The script then repeatedly divides that page value by \(N\), collecting the remainders as digits. It fills from right to left so that leading zero digits are retained as the alphabet’s first character. This is ordinary positional notation, applied to a fixed-width field.

The difference is substantial, and the clause does not say which rate controls. A customer encountering this term in a standardized agreement could reasonably expect the written percentage and its spelled-out equivalent to match. The inconsistency therefore obscures the financial obligation rather than clearly disclosing it, making C the best example of a term that hides or ambiguously states a material service-contract charge.

The ambiguity matters because the clause makes late charges apply to unpaid amounts and then adds that all fees are “non-refundable and payable in advance.” Those are separate financial terms, but their placement alongside the conflicting rate may make it harder for a customer to understand the consequences of signing. In an adhesion-contract setting, the customer generally has little or no opportunity to negotiate standardized language. Under the doctrine of reasonable expectations, a court may be less willing to enforce an unexpected or unclear burden where the drafter could readily have stated it unambiguously. The discrepancy does not, by itself, establish that a court would strike the clause; the outcome would depend on applicable law and the agreement’s context. But it is the clearest anomalous and potentially deceptive feature among the options.

```python
import math
import numpy as np
from scipy.constants import Avogadro, Boltzmann


def velocity_verlet_berendsen(
    N, xyz, v_xyz, L, sigma, epsilon, rc, m, dt,
    tau_T, T_target, tau_P, P_target
):
    """
    Advance a periodic Lennard-Jones system by one velocity-Verlet step,
    optionally applying Berendsen temperature and pressure coupling.

    Units:
        xyz, L, sigma, rc : nm
        v_xyz             : nm/ps
        epsilon           : zJ per particle
        m                 : g/mol
        dt, tau_T, tau_P   : ps
        T_target           : K
        P_target           : bar

    Returns:
        xyz_full, v_xyz_full, L
    """
    xyz = np.asarray(xyz, dtype=float).copy()
    v_xyz = np.asarray(v_xyz, dtype=float).copy()

    if xyz.shape != (N, 3) or v_xyz.shape != (N, 3):
        raise ValueError("xyz and v_xyz must both have shape (N, 3).")
    if N < 2:
        raise ValueError("At least two particles are required.")
    if L <= 0 or dt <= 0 or m <= 0 or sigma <= 0 or rc <= 0:
        raise ValueError("L, dt, m, sigma, and rc must be positive.")
    if tau_T < 0 or tau_P < 0:
        raise ValueError("Thermostat and barostat time constants cannot be negative.")
    if rc > L / 2:
        raise ValueError("For the minimum-image convention, rc must be <= L/2.")

    # Convert the mass and energy to units compatible with nm and ps.
    # 1 g/mol = 1.660539...e-3 zJ ps^2/nm^2.
    mass_internal = m * 1.0e-3 * Avogadro * 1.0e-21
    # 1 zJ = 1e-21 J = 1e-21 kg m^2/s^2.
    # In g/mol, nm, ps units, 1 zJ = 1e-3 * Avogadro * 1e-21.
    energy_to_internal = 1.0e-3 * Avogadro * 1.0e-21

    # Boltzmann constant in zJ/K.
    kB_zJ = Boltzmann * 1.0e21

    def lj_force_and_potential(positions, box_length):
        """Return forces (zJ/nm) and potential energy (zJ)."""
        forces = np.zeros_like(positions)
        potential = 0.0
        inv_box = 1.0 / box_length

        for i in range(N - 1):
            dr = positions[i] - positions[i + 1:]
            dr -= box_length * np.rint(dr * inv_box)

            r2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", dr, dr)
            within = (r2 < rc * rc) & (r2 > 0.0)
            if not np.any(within):
                continue

            rij = dr[within]
            r2 = r2[within]
            inv_r2 = 1.0 / r2
            sr2 = sigma * sigma * inv_r2
            sr6 = sr2 ** 3
            sr12 = sr6 ** 2

            # Force-shifted truncated LJ potential:
            # U_fs(r) = U(r) - U(rc) + (r - rc) F(rc).
            # This makes both the potential and force continuous at rc.
            frc = 24.0 * epsilon / rc * (
                2.0 * (sigma / rc) ** 12 - (sigma / rc) ** 6
            )
            rc6 = (sigma / rc) ** 6
            uc = 4.0 * epsilon * (rc6 * rc6 - rc6)

            r = np.sqrt(r2)
            u = 4.0 * epsilon * (sr12 - sr6) - uc + (r - rc) * frc
            f_over_r = (
                24.0 * epsilon * (2.0 * sr12 - sr6) / r2 - frc / r
            )
            fij = f_over_r[:, None] * rij

            potential += np.sum(u)
            forces[i] += np.sum(fij, axis=0)
            forces[i + 1:][within] -= fij

        return forces, potential

    def kinetic_temperature(velocities):
        kinetic = 0.5 * mass_internal * np.sum(velocities ** 2)
        dof = 3 * N - 3  # remove center-of-mass degrees of freedom
        temperature = (
            2.0 * kinetic / (dof * kB_zJ)
            if dof > 0 else 0.0
        )
        return kinetic, temperature

    def instantaneous_pressure(velocities, forces):
        """Pressure in bar, using the virial expression."""
        volume = L ** 3
        kinetic, _ = kinetic_temperature(velocities)

        # Pair virial: sum over i<j of r_ij . F_ij.
        virial = 0.0
        for i in range(N - 1):
            dr = xyz[i] - xyz[i + 1:]
            dr -= L * np.rint(dr / L)
            r2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", dr, dr)
            within = (r2 < rc * rc) & (r2 > 0.0)
            if np.any(within):
                virial += np.sum(np.einsum("ij,ij->i", dr[within], forces[i + 1:][within]))

        # Internal pressure is zJ/nm^3. 1 zJ/nm^3 = 1e6 Pa = 10 bar.
        pressure_internal = (2.0 * kinetic + virial) / (3.0 * volume)
        return 10.0 * pressure_internal

    # Initial force and acceleration.
    forces, _ = lj_force_and_potential(xyz, L)
    acceleration = forces / mass_internal

    # Velocity-Verlet position update.
    xyz_full = xyz + v_xyz * dt + 0.5 * acceleration * dt * dt
    xyz_full %= L

    # Compute forces at the updated positions.
    forces_new, _ = lj_force_and_potential(xyz_full, L)
    acceleration_new = forces_new / mass_internal

    # Velocity-Verlet velocity update.
    v_xyz_full = v_xyz + 0.5 * (acceleration + acceleration_new) * dt

    # Berendsen thermostat.
    if tau_T > 0:
        _, temperature = kinetic_temperature(v_xyz_full)
        if temperature > 0:
            scale_T = math.sqrt(
                max(0.0, 1.0 + (dt / tau_T) * (T_target / temperature - 1.0))
            )
            v_xyz_full *= scale_T

    # Berendsen barostat.  The virial pressure is evaluated at the current
    # box size and the already thermostat-scaled velocities.
    if tau_P > 0:
        pressure = instantaneous_pressure(v_xyz_full, forces_new)
        # Berendsen isotropic scaling requires an isothermal compressibility.
        # This simple LJ implementation uses a configurable default value in
        # bar^-1; replace it with a value appropriate for the system.
        beta_T = 1.0e-4  # bar^-1
        scale_P = 1.0 - (dt / tau_P) * beta_T * (P_target - pressure)
        if scale_P <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Barostat produced a non-positive box scaling factor.")

        length_scale = scale_P ** (1.0 / 3.0)
        L_new = L * length_scale

        if L_new < 2.0 * rc:
            raise Exception(
                "Berendsen barostat shrank the box below twice the cutoff radius."
            )

        xyz_full *= length_scale
        xyz_full %= L_new
        L = L_new

    return xyz_full, v_xyz_full, L
```

```python
# Standard Lorenz-system parameters

def lorenz(state):

    x, y, z = state
    return np.array([

        x * (RHO - z) - y,
        x * y - BETA * z,
    ], dtype=float)

    k2 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k1)
    k3 = lorenz(state + 0.5 * dt * k2)

    for i in range(len(times) - 1):
```

The Lorenz system defines a deterministic flow in three-dimensional phase space, where each point \((x,y,z)\) specifies the system’s complete state at a given time. A phase-space trajectory is the curve traced by that state as the differential equations evolve it. For the standard parameters \(\sigma=10\), \(\beta=8/3\), and \(\rho=28\), trajectories are drawn toward a bounded, intricate invariant set known as the Lorenz attractor. Its familiar two-lobed appearance reflects the way trajectories move around one lobe, pass through a central region, and then continue around either lobe. The attractor is “strange” in the dynamical-systems sense: it has a complex, non-smooth geometry and supports sensitive, non-periodic motion, even though the governing equations are smooth and deterministic.

The script integrates two trajectories with the same \(y\) and \(z\) coordinates but slightly different \(x\) coordinates. Classical RK4 approximates each time step by combining four derivative evaluations, giving fourth-order accuracy for a sufficiently small fixed step. The plotted distance is the Euclidean norm
\[
d(t)=\|\mathbf{x}_A(t)-\mathbf{x}_B(t)\|_2,
\]
where \(\mathbf{x}_A\) and \(\mathbf{x}_B\) are the two state vectors. Initially, this distance is \(10^{-4}\); as the solutions evolve, it will generally grow substantially before remaining bounded by the attractor’s finite extent. This growth illustrates sensitivity to initial conditions: small uncertainties in a starting state can eventually lead to large differences in predicted states. The precise separation curve depends on the initial conditions and numerical settings, and finite precision and integration error also affect long-time comparisons.

For a deterministic system with flow map \(\Phi^t\), the maximal Lyapunov exponent measures the largest asymptotic exponential rate at which infinitesimally nearby states separate. In a common formulation, for a perturbation vector \(\delta\mathbf{x}(0)\),
\[
\lambda_{\max}
=\limsup_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}
\ln\!\left(
\frac{\|D\Phi^t(\mathbf{x}_0)\,\delta\mathbf{x}(0)\|}
{\|\delta\mathbf{x}(0)\|}
\right),
\]
where \(D\Phi^t\) is the derivative of the flow with respect to its initial state. A positive maximal exponent indicates exponential divergence along at least one direction for typical nearby states and is a hallmark of chaos; a negative exponent indicates contraction in every direction, while a zero exponent can correspond to neutral evolution. The distance plotted by this script is a useful qualitative demonstration, not by itself a reliable Lyapunov-exponent estimate: finite perturbations eventually leave the linear-growth regime, and a robust numerical estimate typically requires repeated renormalization of perturbations or an appropriate variational-equation method.

The Lorenz attractor is a geometric structure in the system’s three-dimensional phase space, whose coordinates are the state variables \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\). For the standard parameters \(\sigma=10\), \(\beta=8/3\), and \(\rho=28\), trajectories are drawn toward a bounded, intricate set with two prominent lobes. A trajectory may loop around one lobe before moving to the other, but it does not settle into a fixed point or repeat as a simple periodic orbit. The resulting “butterfly” appearance is a projection of the attractor’s folded, layered geometry: nearby states can be stretched apart along some directions and compressed along others while remaining confined overall. The attractor is not a surface that the system is externally constrained to follow; it is an invariant set approached by many initial states, with its geometry arising from the flow defined by the differential equations.

A phase-space trajectory records the evolving state \((x(t),y(t),z(t))\), rather than the motion of an object through ordinary physical space. The script approximates this flow with classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration, advancing each state through small time steps using weighted evaluations of the differential equations. It then compares two trajectories with nearly identical initial conditions by computing their Euclidean separation,
\[
d(t)=\left\|\mathbf{u}_A(t)-\mathbf{u}_B(t)\right\|_2,
\qquad \mathbf{u}=(x,y,z).
\]
In a chaotic regime, this separation typically grows rapidly for an initial interval, illustrating sensitivity to initial conditions. Because the attractor is bounded, the distance does not grow without limit: it can fluctuate and eventually become comparable to the attractor’s overall scale. The numerical comparison therefore demonstrates finite-time divergence, not an indefinitely increasing distance. Its precise appearance depends on integration duration, step size, and floating-point precision.

For a deterministic flow \(\dot{\mathbf{u}}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})\), the maximal Lyapunov exponent measures the mean asymptotic exponential growth rate of an infinitesimal perturbation in the most rapidly expanding direction. In a common continuous-time definition, if \(\delta\mathbf{u}(0)\) is a sufficiently small perturbation and \(\delta\mathbf{u}(t)\) is its evolution under the linearized dynamics, then
\[
\lambda_{\max}
=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}
\ln\!\left(\frac{\|\delta\mathbf{u}(t)\|}
{\|\delta\mathbf{u}(0)\|}\right),
\]
when the limit exists for the trajectory under consideration. A positive maximal exponent indicates exponential sensitivity and is a standard signature of chaos; a negative one indicates contraction in all directions, while zero can occur along a neutral direction such as the direction of motion on a continuous-time orbit. In computation, one estimates the exponent over finite intervals and typically rescales perturbations to prevent them from becoming too large. The separation plot in this script is a useful qualitative demonstration, but by itself is not a reliable long-time Lyapunov-exponent estimate.

```python
import numpy as np
from rdkit import Chem, DataStructs
from rdkit.Chem import rdFingerprintGenerator

smiles = {

    "Caffeine": "CN1C=NC2=C1C(=O)N(C(=O)N2C)C",

molecules = {}
for name, text in smiles.items():
    mol = Chem.MolFromSmiles(text)
    if mol is None:
        raise ValueError(f"Could not parse SMILES for {name}")
    molecules[name] = mol

# Build and print each molecule's atom-by-atom topological adjacency matrix.
# Entry (i, j) is 1 if atoms i and j share a bond, otherwise 0.
for name, mol in molecules.items():
    adjacency = Chem.GetAdjacencyMatrix(mol)
    print(f"\n{name} adjacency matrix ({adjacency.shape[0]} atoms):")
    print(adjacency)

# ECFP4 corresponds to a Morgan fingerprint with radius 2.
# A fixed-size bit vector is convenient for pairwise Tanimoto calculations.
generator = rdFingerprintGenerator.GetMorganGenerator(radius=2, fpSize=2048)
fingerprints = {
    name: generator.GetFingerprint(mol)
    for name, mol in molecules.items()
}

# Compute and print the symmetric pairwise Tanimoto similarity matrix.
names = list(molecules)
similarity_matrix = np.eye(len(names))

for i, j in combinations(range(len(names)), 2):
    similarity = DataStructs.TanimotoSimilarity(
        fingerprints[names[i]], fingerprints[names[j]]
    )
    similarity_matrix[i, j] = similarity_matrix[j, i] = similarity

print("\nPairwise ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity matrix:")
print("            " + "  ".join(f"{name:>10}" for name in names))
for name, row in zip(names, similarity_matrix):
    print(f"{name:>10}  " + "  ".join(f"{value:10.4f}" for value in row))
```

A molecular graph represents a molecule as \(G=(V,E)\), where vertices \(V\) are atoms and edges \(E\) are bonds. Its adjacency matrix \(A\) has \(A_{ij}=1\) when atoms \(i\) and \(j\) are directly bonded and \(A_{ij}=0\) otherwise; the diagonal is zero for these ordinary molecular graphs. An ECFP4 fingerprint is a circular, atom-centered encoding that iteratively summarizes local environments to a radius of two bonds. Initially, each atom receives an identifier based on properties such as its element, degree, valence, formal charge, and hydrogen count. At each iteration, an atom’s identifier is updated by combining its previous identifier with the identifiers and bond types of its neighboring atoms. The resulting identifiers describe environments extending progressively farther from each atom. These identifiers are then mapped into a fixed-length bit vector. Thus, the fingerprint records a collection of local structural features rather than preserving the complete molecular graph; hashing into a finite vector can also cause distinct features to occupy the same bit.

For binary fingerprints \(A\) and \(B\), let \(a\) and \(b\) denote their numbers of set bits and \(c\) the number of bits set in both. Their Tanimoto similarity is
\[
T(A,B)=\frac{c}{a+b-c},
\]
the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of their feature sets. It ranges from 0 (no shared set bits) to 1 (identical bit sets). The corresponding Jaccard distance is \(1-T(A,B)\). In the script, RDKit computes this coefficient directly from each pair of ECFP4 bit vectors, and the results form a symmetric matrix with ones on the diagonal. Because fingerprint bits are hashed representations of environments, a high score indicates substantial overlap under this representation; it does not prove that two molecules have identical structures or biological effects.

Similarity thresholds in virtual screening are practical ranking conventions, not universal definitions of chemical equivalence. A threshold near 0.7 is sometimes used to identify close analogues in particular fingerprint-based searches, while lower cutoffs can retrieve broader, more diverse candidate sets; the useful value depends on the fingerprint, dataset, assay, and objective. In medicinal chemistry, analogues with high fingerprint similarity may be useful for lead optimization, whereas lower-similarity compounds can help explore new chemical space. Importantly, the similarity–activity relationship is not guaranteed: small structural changes can alter potency, selectivity, solubility, or toxicity, and similar fingerprints can mask differences in three-dimensional shape or context. Scores should therefore be interpreted alongside scaffold analysis, physicochemical properties, biological data, and validation appropriate to the screening task.

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import find_peaks

# Signal parameters
sample_rate = 44_100
duration = 1.0
t = np.arange(int(sample_rate * duration)) / sample_rate

# C-major triad fundamentals: C4, E4, G4
fundamentals = {
    "C4": 261.63,
    "E4": 329.63,
    "G4": 392.00,
}

# Relative amplitudes for the fundamental, 2nd harmonic, and 3rd harmonic.
# The harmonics decay logarithmically with harmonic number.
harmonic_numbers = np.array([1, 2, 3])
harmonic_amplitudes = 1.0 / np.log2(harmonic_numbers + 1)

# Synthesize and mix the notes and their first two overtones.
signal = np.zeros_like(t)
for fundamental in fundamentals.values():
    for harmonic, amplitude in zip(harmonic_numbers, harmonic_amplitudes):
        signal += amplitude * np.sin(
            2 * np.pi * fundamental * harmonic * t
        )

# Avoid clipping if the signal is played or saved as audio.
signal /= np.max(np.abs(signal))

# Apply a Hann window to reduce spectral leakage at the signal boundaries.
windowed_signal = signal * np.hanning(len(signal))

# Compute the one-sided amplitude spectrum.
spectrum = np.fft.rfft(windowed_signal)
frequencies = np.fft.rfftfreq(len(windowed_signal), d=1 / sample_rate)
magnitudes = np.abs(spectrum)

# Find local spectral peaks. The threshold suppresses small numerical
# or window-related peaks while retaining the synthesized partials.
peak_indices, _ = find_peaks(
    magnitudes,
    height=np.max(magnitudes) * 0.01,
    distance=max(1, int(5 * duration)),
)

# Print the strongest peaks, ordered by frequency.
print("Detected frequency peaks (Hz):")
for index in sorted(peak_indices, key=lambda i: frequencies[i]):
    print(f"{frequencies[index]:8.2f} Hz")
```

The script constructs a one-second discrete-time signal by sampling each note at 44.1 kHz and adding its fundamental and second and third harmonics. The chosen harmonic amplitudes, \(1/\log_2(h+1)\), decrease as harmonic number \(h\) increases. Because the specified note frequencies are not generally exact integer multiples of the FFT’s frequency-bin spacing for a one-second record, detected peak locations may differ slightly from the nominal frequencies. The Hann window reduces spectral leakage, but does not change the underlying frequencies.

The Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) represents a finite sequence of samples as a weighted sum of complex sinusoids. For a sequence \(x[n]\) of \(N\) samples, its DFT is \(X[k]=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\), where \(k\) indexes discrete frequency bins. Each complex coefficient records both the strength and phase of the corresponding sinusoidal component; taking \(|X[k]|\) yields a magnitude spectrum useful for locating prominent frequencies. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is an efficient algorithm for computing this same DFT, not a different transform. For a sample rate \(f_s\), bin \(k\) corresponds to \(k f_s/N\) Hz, so the bin spacing is \(f_s/N\). Here, \(N=44{,}100\), giving 1 Hz spacing. A finite observation effectively truncates the signal; if its endpoints do not align with sinusoidal cycles, energy spreads into neighboring bins, an effect called spectral leakage.

Timbre is the perceptual quality that lets listeners distinguish sounds with similar pitch and loudness. For a periodic tone, the fundamental frequency establishes the perceived pitch, while partials at integer multiples of that frequency form its harmonic spectrum. Their relative amplitudes—and, in many contexts, their evolution over time—strongly influence timbre. A sound with strong upper harmonics may be perceived as brighter or sharper than one dominated by its fundamental. Instruments also differ in inharmonic components, noise, attack, and decay, so a static harmonic mixture is a useful simplification rather than a complete model of an instrument. In the synthesized triad, each note contributes energy at its own fundamental and at twice and three times that frequency. Some partials from different notes can lie near one another, but the FFT can still reveal the separate spectral peaks when frequency resolution and signal-to-noise conditions are adequate.

Time and frequency resolution are constrained by the time-frequency uncertainty principle, often discussed in DSP as the Gabor limit. Informally, a signal cannot be localized arbitrarily precisely in both time and frequency: a short analysis window gives good temporal localization but a broad frequency response, whereas a long window gives sharper frequency discrimination but averages over a longer time. For a windowed Fourier analysis, this trade-off is reflected in the window’s time spread and frequency spread; their product has a nonzero lower bound whose exact form depends on the definitions and window. Thus, increasing the FFT length does not create unlimited information: it typically requires observing a longer segment or adding assumptions such as zero-padding, which interpolates the displayed spectrum without improving true resolving power. The one-second, 1 Hz-bin analysis here is suitable for identifying stable triad partials, but would be less suitable for pinpointing the rapid pitch and spectral changes of a short musical attack.

```python
from random import Random
from time import perf_counter


class NaiveArray:
    """Point updates and range sums using a Python list."""

    def __init__(self, values):
        self.data = values.copy()

    def update(self, index, value):
        self.data[index] = value

    def range_sum(self, left, right):
        # Inclusive endpoints
        return sum(self.data[left:right + 1])


class SegmentTree:
    """Iterative segment tree supporting point updates and inclusive range sums."""

    def __init__(self, values):
        self.n = len(values)
        self.tree = [0] * (2 * self.n)

        # Leaves occupy tree[n:2*n].
        self.tree[self.n:] = values

        # Build internal nodes bottom-up.
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]

    def update(self, index, value):
        pos = index + self.n
        self.tree[pos] = value

        pos //= 2
        while pos:
            self.tree[pos] = self.tree[2 * pos] + self.tree[2 * pos + 1]
            pos //= 2

    def range_sum(self, left, right):
        """Return the sum over the inclusive interval [left, right]."""
        left += self.n
        right += self.n + 1  # Convert to a half-open interval [left, right).

        total = 0
        while left < right:
            if left & 1:
                total += self.tree[left]
                left += 1
            if right & 1:
                right -= 1
                total += self.tree[right]
            left //= 2
            right //= 2

        return total


def make_operations(n, q, seed=2025):
    """Generate a shared, deterministic sequence of updates and queries."""
    rng = Random(seed)
    operations = []

    for _ in range(q):
        if rng.random() < 0.5:
            index = rng.randrange(n)
            value = rng.randrange(-1000, 1001)
            operations.append(("update", index, value))
        else:
            left = rng.randrange(n)
            right = rng.randrange(left, n)
            operations.append(("query", left, right))

    return operations


def run_benchmark():
    n = 100_000
    q = 50_000
    rng = Random(12345)
    initial = [rng.randrange(-1000, 1001) for _ in range(n)]
    operations = make_operations(n, q)

    # Time the naive implementation.
    naive = NaiveArray(initial)
    naive_query_checksum = 0
    start = perf_counter()
    for operation in operations:
        if operation[0] == "update":
            _, index, value = operation
            naive.update(index, value)
        else:
            _, left, right = operation
            naive_query_checksum += naive.range_sum(left, right)
    naive_seconds = perf_counter() - start

    # Time the segment tree implementation.
    segment_tree = SegmentTree(initial)
    tree_query_checksum = 0
    start = perf_counter()
    for operation in operations:
        if operation[0] == "update":
            _, index, value = operation
            segment_tree.update(index, value)
        else:
            _, left, right = operation
            tree_query_checksum += segment_tree.range_sum(left, right)
    tree_seconds = perf_counter() - start

    # Identical checksums verify that both implementations processed the
    # same operations and returned matching query results.
    assert naive_query_checksum == tree_query_checksum

    print(f"N = {n:,}, operations = {q:,}")
    print(f"Naive array:  {naive_seconds:.3f} seconds")
    print(f"Segment tree: {tree_seconds:.3f} seconds")
    if tree_seconds > 0:
        print(f"Speedup:      {naive_seconds / tree_seconds:.1f}x")
    print(f"Query checksum: {tree_query_checksum}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_benchmark()
```

The naive array stores the values in a contiguous Python list. A point update takes **Θ(1)** time, while a range-sum query on an interval of length \(k\) takes **Θ(k)** time because it must inspect every element. Thus, for \(U\) updates and queries of lengths \(k_1,\ldots,k_R\), the total work is **Θ(\(U+\sum_{i=1}^{R} k_i\))**; in the worst case, this is **Θ(\(U+RN\))**, or **Θ(\(QN\))** when the operation mix is considered as a whole. The list uses **Θ(N)** space. By contrast, the segment tree uses **Θ(N)** space and performs both point updates and range queries in **Θ(log N)** time, giving **Θ(N + Q log N)** total work after construction. These are tight bounds for this implementation: updates visit a root-to-leaf path, and queries may require processing a logarithmic number of tree nodes, so their worst-case costs are both **Θ(log N)** (and therefore also **O(log N)** and **Ω(log N)** in the worst case).

For a recursive tree over \(N\) elements, construction obeys the recurrence \(T(N)=T(\lfloor N/2\rfloor)+T(\lceil N/2\rceil)+\Theta(1)\), with \(T(1)=\Theta(1)\). Each internal node performs constant work after constructing its two children, so the tree has \(N\) leaves and \(N-1\) internal nodes; consequently, construction is **Θ(N)**. A traversal that follows one root-to-leaf path obeys \(S(N)=S(\lceil N/2\rceil)+\Theta(1)\), with \(S(1)=\Theta(1)\), and hence takes **Θ(log N)**. To see the height bound formally, after \(h\) balanced splits, a subproblem has size at most \(\lceil N/2^h\rceil\). Choosing \(h=\lceil\log_2 N\rceil\) makes this size at most one, so the height is at most \(\lceil\log_2 N\rceil\); conversely, a binary tree with \(N\) leaves must have height at least \(\lceil\log_2 N\rceil\), since height \(h\) can accommodate at most \(2^h\) leaves. Therefore the height is **Θ(log N)**. Range queries visit only the boundary paths and fully covered subtrees; at each level, only a constant number of nodes need further consideration, yielding **O(log N)** traversal work.

Asymptotic bounds describe growth, not elapsed time on a particular machine. A Python segment tree has extra list slots, index arithmetic, loop branches, and object-reference overhead; its storage can therefore consume substantially more physical memory than the underlying array, despite both structures being **Θ(N)**.
